approachQuestion.prompt:
Rectangle audit. A fixed R by C grid records signed adjustments. Each of q requests (top, left, bottom, right) asks for the sum inside that inclusive rectangle. Return q sums in request order.

Input: grid [[3, -1, 4], [2, 5, -2]], requests [(0,1,1,2), (1,0,1,0)]. Output: [6, 2].

Constraints: 1 ≤ R,C ≤ 1000; 1 ≤ q ≤ 200000. Every rectangle is valid and nonempty, with zero-based coordinates. Cells are integers between -1000000 and 1000000. The grid is read-only. All arithmetic fits signed 64-bit integers.

Which approach handles the complete task correctly and efficiently?

options.text: Build P with a leading zero row and column, where P[i][j] totals rows before i and columns before j. Answer a rectangle using P[bottom+1][right+1] - P[top][right+1] - P[bottom+1][left] + P[top][left].
options.feedback: Subtract the two outside strips and restore their overlap, which was subtracted twice.

options.text: Build a cumulative array for each row; for every request, sum its row-range answers from top through bottom.
options.feedback: This is correct for every rectangle, but visits every covered row per request. A table over both dimensions removes that repeated work.

options.text: Use the same P, but subtract the upper and left strips without adding P[top][left].
options.feedback: The strips overlap. On [[1,2],[3,4]], querying only cell (1,1) produces 3 instead of 4.

options.text: Visit every cell in each requested rectangle and sum it.
options.feedback: The totals are correct, but repeated large rectangles revisit the entire grid for each request.

feedback.reason: Build a table of totals from the origin to each boundary. For each rectangle, take the total through its bottom-right boundary, subtract the upper and left strips, and add back their shared corner.
details: Build a table of totals from the origin to each boundary. For each rectangle, take the total through its bottom-right boundary, subtract the upper and left strips, and add back their shared corner.
Subtracting the upper and left strips removes their shared corner twice. Add that corner back once. A zero border handles rectangles touching the first row or column without negative indices.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the method in the reveal. Choose its tightest worst-case time and worst-case auxiliary-space pair. Use constant-time 64-bit arithmetic. Include the allocated table; exclude the supplied grid, requests and required output array. The method is iterative and copies no grid.

options.text: O(RC + q) time; O(RC) auxiliary space
O(RC + Rq) time; O(RC) auxiliary space
O(RC + q) time; O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Build the two-dimensional table and perform four boundary reads per rectangle.
details: Fill each table cell once and read four entries per request.
Use constant-time 64-bit arithmetic. Include the allocated table; exclude the supplied grid, requests and required output array. The method is iterative and copies no grid.
The (R+1)(C+1) entries require O(RC) space; loop variables use constant space and no recursive stack.
Row tables cost O(RC+Rq) worst-case time; scanning rectangles costs O(RCq). Neither matches the target batch time.

methodReveal.title: Combine four corners
methodReveal.description: Build a table of totals from the origin to each boundary. For each rectangle, take the total through its bottom-right boundary, subtract the upper and left strips, and add back their shared corner.
